passages.title: Cyrus permits return
passages.summary: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, the LORD stirs the king’s spirit. Cyrus sends a written order through his kingdom. He says the God of heaven has told him to build a house in Jerusalem. Any of God’s people may go up and build it. Their neighbors are to help with silver, gold, goods, and animals. Family heads, priests, and Levites prepare to go. Cyrus brings out the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar took. They are counted out to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Ezra names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies how people outside the community can help God’s work. Who is invited to go up in verse 3?

contextNote.title: Return occurs within Persian rule
contextNote.text: Verse 1 credits the LORD with moving a foreign king. Verse 3 makes the return a matter of choice: “Whoever there is among you.” Verse 5 says those went whose spirit God had stirred. Permission comes from the ruler of the whole region. No king of Judah is restored, and worship resumes without independence. Verses 7–11 count the old vessels to link the new house with the first. The Cyrus Cylinder provides wider royal context without naming Judah’s returning families.

passages.title: The returning community
passages.summary: This chapter lists the people who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. Families are counted by ancestor and by home town. Priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants follow. Some families cannot prove that they belong to Israel. Some priests cannot find their family records. The governor bars them from the holy food until a priest can decide. The whole company numbers 42,360, with servants and singers besides. Family heads give gold, silver, and priestly garments for the work.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Ezra names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Seminary introduction describes the families returning from exile, or forced life abroad. What do their gifts help rebuild?

contextNote.title: Belonging requires more than arrival
contextNote.text: After the exile, written records show who may serve as a priest. Verse 62 says some priestly families searched and found nothing. They are removed from the priesthood for the present. Verse 63 leaves the final decision to a priest with Urim and Thummim. So the ruling is a suspension, not a last word. Lay families with the same problem are listed and not sent away (verses 59–60). The line is drawn most strictly at the altar.

passages.title: Altar, foundations, joy, and grief
passages.summary: In the seventh month the people gather in Jerusalem as one. Jeshua and Zerubbabel build the altar on its old base. They fear the neighboring peoples and offer sacrifices morning and evening. They keep the Feast of Booths before any foundation is laid. They pay masons and carpenters and order cedar from Lebanon. In the second year the builders lay the temple’s foundation. Priests blow trumpets, and Levites sing that the LORD is good. Old men who saw the first house weep while others shout for joy.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Ezra names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me considers the joy and grief accompanying temple rebuilding. Who weeps in verse 12, and why?

contextNote.title: A foundation holds two different memories
contextNote.text: The altar comes first, before walls or roof (verses 2–3). Worship does not wait for a finished building. When the foundation is laid, two sounds rise together. Verse 12 says the old men who remembered the first house wept aloud. Others shouted for joy. Verse 13 says no one could tell the two sounds apart. The text corrects neither group, and Haggai 2:3 speaks to the same grief.

passages.title: Opposition and royal letters
passages.summary: Neighbors of Judah and Benjamin offer to help build the temple. Zerubbabel and the leaders refuse. The neighbors then discourage the builders and hire advisers against them. This continues from the reign of Cyrus to that of Darius. Later, officials write to King Artaxerxes about Jerusalem’s walls. They call it a rebellious city that will stop paying taxes. The king searches the records and orders the building to stop. Work on God’s house ceases until the second year of Darius.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: The points show chosen known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and Achmetha have no points because their locations are not known here.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies responses to opposition. What does the king order in verse 21, and what does he leave open?

contextNote.title: Opposition does not follow a simple sequence
contextNote.text: The chapter groups disputes from several reigns. It names Cyrus, Darius, Ahasuerus, Artaxerxes, and Darius again (verses 5–7, 24). The letter in verses 12–16 concerns the city walls, not the temple. A clay bulla of the Persian period shows how documents were sealed. Opposition is the theme that holds these events together. The order in verse 21 stops the work by force of law. It also leaves room for a later decree to change it.

passages.title: Prophets encourage work as officials ask questions
passages.summary: The prophets Haggai and Zechariah speak to the Jews in God’s name. Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin again to build the house. Tattenai, the governor west of the River, asks who authorized them. He takes down the builders’ names. The work continues while he writes to King Darius. His letter reports the elders’ answer in full. They say Cyrus ordered the house rebuilt and returned its vessels. Tattenai asks the king to search the royal archives.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Ezra names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how the people continue God’s work despite opposition. How do the elders identify themselves in verse 11?

contextNote.title: Local builders answer through a longer history
contextNote.text: The elders answer an official inquiry in verse 11. They say whose servants they are and that a great king built it. The governor sends a letter (verse 6); a bulla shows how letters were sealed. Verse 12 admits that their fathers angered God and lost it. That explains the ruin without saying their God was weak. Verse 13 gives the legal ground: a decree of Cyrus. The dispute is about who may authorize building inside the empire.

passages.title: The king's order, the temple, and Passover
passages.summary: Darius orders a search of the archives. A scroll is found in the fortress of Achmetha in Media. It records Cyrus’s decree, with the temple’s size and the crown’s payment. Darius tells Tattenai to leave the work alone. He orders the costs paid from the region’s taxes. He supplies animals, wheat, salt, wine, and oil for the offerings. The elders finish the house in the sixth year of Darius. They dedicate it with joy and keep the Passover.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: The points show chosen known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and Achmetha have no points because their locations are not known here.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the temple's opening and the people's joy. Where is the scroll found in verse 2?

contextNote.title: A stored record changes a local dispute
contextNote.text: The search begins in Babylon, and the record turns up in Media (verses 1–2). A clay bulla of the Persian period shows how documents were sealed. A stored memo answers the charges of local opponents. Darius goes beyond what the Jews asked and pays the costs (verses 8–9). In verse 10 he wants prayers for himself and his sons. So permission brings duties and royal oversight with it. Verse 14 credits the result to prophets, God’s command, and Persian kings together.

passages.title: Ezra studies the law and receives royal support
passages.summary: Years later Ezra comes up from Babylon. He is a priest of Aaron’s line and a scribe skilled in Moses’s law. King Artaxerxes grants all he asks. The journey takes about four months. The king’s letter lets any Israelite go with him. It sends silver and gold for offerings and frees temple workers from tax. It tells Ezra to appoint judges and teach God’s laws. Ezra blesses the LORD, who put this in the king’s heart.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Ezra names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church lesson joins scripture study with practice and teaching. What three things had Ezra set his heart to do (verse 10)?

contextNote.title: Teaching joins study with conduct
contextNote.text: Verse 10 gives three verbs in a fixed order. Ezra set his heart to seek the law, to do it, and to teach it. Study comes first, and practice stands between study and teaching. Verses 6 and 9 say God’s hand was on him. The king’s letter then gives him wide powers (verses 25–26). He may appoint judges and enforce both God’s law and the king’s. Ezra credits God, not himself, for the king’s favor (verses 27–28).

passages.title: Prayer, travel, and the care of temple gifts
passages.summary: Ezra lists the family heads who travel with him. At the river Ahava he finds no Levites in the camp. He sends for some, and Levites and temple servants join. He calls a fast and asks God for a safe road. He is ashamed to ask the king for soldiers. He weighs the silver, gold, and vessels into the hands of twelve priests. They reach Jerusalem safely. On the fourth day everything is weighed again and written down.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Ezra names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson studies fasting, prayer, and trust before the journey. What must the priests do with the gifts in verse 29?

contextNote.title: Sacred gifts need public accountability
contextNote.text: Ezra had told the king that God protects those who seek him (verse 22). So he will not ask for an armed escort. His trust does not remove the need to weigh the gifts. Named guardians receive them by weight before travel (verses 24–27). Verse 29 tells them to guard them until the next weighing. Verses 33–34 report matching counts and a written record. A trade weight shows the kind of tool used for such weighing.

passages.title: Ezra prays about the mixed marriages
passages.summary: Leaders tell Ezra that the people have married among the neighboring peoples. Priests, Levites, and officials are among them. Ezra tears his clothes and sits appalled until the evening offering. Then he kneels and prays. He says the people’s guilt has grown up to the heavens. God has given them a little relief and a foothold in his holy place. They are still servants under Persia’s kings. He asks how they can break the commandments again.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: The points show chosen known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and Achmetha have no points because their locations are not known here.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects these marriages with worship of other gods. Ezra gives no personal testimony from the wives. How does Ezra describe his people’s condition in verse 9?

contextNote.title: Gratitude and fear shape the prayer
contextNote.text: Ezra says “we” and “our” through the whole prayer. He has not made these marriages himself. Verse 8 says God will “revive us a little.” Verse 9 says the people are still bondservants under Persian kings. Yet God has shown them kindness and let them rebuild. Ezra fears this small survival could be lost (verse 14). Deuteronomy 7:3–4 gives the law’s stated concern: turning to other gods.

passages.title: The marriage investigation
passages.summary: While Ezra prays and weeps, a large crowd gathers and weeps with him. Shecaniah proposes a covenant to send away the foreign wives and their children. Ezra makes the leaders swear to it. All the men are called to Jerusalem within three days. They sit in the open square, trembling in heavy rain. Family heads are chosen to examine each case. The work takes three months. The book ends with a list of the men, and some had children.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: The points show chosen known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and Achmetha have no points because their locations are not known here.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson studies confession and repentance. What voices are missing from the account of separated families?

contextNote.title: A boundary decision has a human cost
contextNote.text: The proposal in verse 3 comes from Shecaniah, not from Ezra. It covers the wives and “those who are born of them.” Verse 15 records four men who opposed the plan. No word from God is reported approving it. The women and children do not speak anywhere in the chapter. The last verse mentions children and then stops (verse 44). Elsewhere the Bible honors Ruth, a woman of Moab (Ruth 4:13–17).

events.title: Altar, foundations, joy, and grief
events.summary: In the seventh month the people gather in Jerusalem as one. Jeshua and Zerubbabel build the altar on its old base. They fear the neighboring peoples and offer sacrifices morning and evening. They keep the Feast of Booths before any foundation is laid. They pay masons and carpenters and order cedar from Lebanon. In the second year the builders lay the temple’s foundation. Priests blow trumpets, and Levites sing that the LORD is good. Old men who saw the first house weep while others shout for joy.
events.detail: The altar comes first, before walls or roof (verses 2–3). Worship does not wait for a finished building. When the foundation is laid, two sounds rise together. Verse 12 says the old men who remembered the first house wept aloud. Others shouted for joy. Verse 13 says no one could tell the two sounds apart. The text corrects neither group, and Haggai 2:3 speaks to the same grief.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me considers the joy and grief accompanying temple rebuilding. Who weeps in verse 12, and why?

events.title: Opposition and royal letters
events.summary: Neighbors of Judah and Benjamin offer to help build the temple. Zerubbabel and the leaders refuse. The neighbors then discourage the builders and hire advisers against them. This continues from the reign of Cyrus to that of Darius. Later, officials write to King Artaxerxes about Jerusalem’s walls. They call it a rebellious city that will stop paying taxes. The king searches the records and orders the building to stop. Work on God’s house ceases until the second year of Darius.
events.detail: The chapter groups disputes from several reigns. It names Cyrus, Darius, Ahasuerus, Artaxerxes, and Darius again (verses 5–7, 24). The letter in verses 12–16 concerns the city walls, not the temple. A clay bulla of the Persian period shows how documents were sealed. Opposition is the theme that holds these events together. The order in verse 21 stops the work by force of law. It also leaves room for a later decree to change it.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies responses to opposition. What does the king order in verse 21, and what does he leave open?

events.title: Prophets encourage work as officials ask questions
events.summary: The prophets Haggai and Zechariah speak to the Jews in God’s name. Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin again to build the house. Tattenai, the governor west of the River, asks who authorized them. He takes down the builders’ names. The work continues while he writes to King Darius. His letter reports the elders’ answer in full. They say Cyrus ordered the house rebuilt and returned its vessels. Tattenai asks the king to search the royal archives.
events.detail: The elders answer an official inquiry in verse 11. They say whose servants they are and that a great king built it. The governor sends a letter (verse 6); a bulla shows how letters were sealed. Verse 12 admits that their fathers angered God and lost it. That explains the ruin without saying their God was weak. Verse 13 gives the legal ground: a decree of Cyrus. The dispute is about who may authorize building inside the empire.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how the people continue God’s work despite opposition. How do the elders identify themselves in verse 11?

events.title: The king's order, the temple, and Passover
events.summary: Darius orders a search of the archives. A scroll is found in the fortress of Achmetha in Media. It records Cyrus’s decree, with the temple’s size and the crown’s payment. Darius tells Tattenai to leave the work alone. He orders the costs paid from the region’s taxes. He supplies animals, wheat, salt, wine, and oil for the offerings. The elders finish the house in the sixth year of Darius. They dedicate it with joy and keep the Passover.
events.detail: The search begins in Babylon, and the record turns up in Media (verses 1–2). A clay bulla of the Persian period shows how documents were sealed. A stored memo answers the charges of local opponents. Darius goes beyond what the Jews asked and pays the costs (verses 8–9). In verse 10 he wants prayers for himself and his sons. So permission brings duties and royal oversight with it. Verse 14 credits the result to prophets, God’s command, and Persian kings together.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the temple's opening and the people's joy. Where is the scroll found in verse 2?

events.title: Ezra studies the law and receives royal support
events.summary: Years later Ezra comes up from Babylon. He is a priest of Aaron’s line and a scribe skilled in Moses’s law. King Artaxerxes grants all he asks. The journey takes about four months. The king’s letter lets any Israelite go with him. It sends silver and gold for offerings and frees temple workers from tax. It tells Ezra to appoint judges and teach God’s laws. Ezra blesses the LORD, who put this in the king’s heart.
events.detail: Verse 10 gives three verbs in a fixed order. Ezra set his heart to seek the law, to do it, and to teach it. Study comes first, and practice stands between study and teaching. Verses 6 and 9 say God’s hand was on him. The king’s letter then gives him wide powers (verses 25–26). He may appoint judges and enforce both God’s law and the king’s. Ezra credits God, not himself, for the king’s favor (verses 27–28).

lds.text: The Church lesson joins scripture study with practice and teaching. What three things had Ezra set his heart to do (verse 10)?

events.title: Prayer, travel, and the care of temple gifts
events.summary: Ezra lists the family heads who travel with him. At the river Ahava he finds no Levites in the camp. He sends for some, and Levites and temple servants join. He calls a fast and asks God for a safe road. He is ashamed to ask the king for soldiers. He weighs the silver, gold, and vessels into the hands of twelve priests. They reach Jerusalem safely. On the fourth day everything is weighed again and written down.
events.detail: Ezra had told the king that God protects those who seek him (verse 22). So he will not ask for an armed escort. His trust does not remove the need to weigh the gifts. Named guardians receive them by weight before travel (verses 24–27). Verse 29 tells them to guard them until the next weighing. Verses 33–34 report matching counts and a written record. A trade weight shows the kind of tool used for such weighing.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson studies fasting, prayer, and trust before the journey. What must the priests do with the gifts in verse 29?

events.title: Ezra prays about the mixed marriages
events.summary: Leaders tell Ezra that the people have married among the neighboring peoples. Priests, Levites, and officials are among them. Ezra tears his clothes and sits appalled until the evening offering. Then he kneels and prays. He says the people’s guilt has grown up to the heavens. God has given them a little relief and a foothold in his holy place. They are still servants under Persia’s kings. He asks how they can break the commandments again.
events.detail: Ezra says “we” and “our” through the whole prayer. He has not made these marriages himself. Verse 8 says God will “revive us a little.” Verse 9 says the people are still bondservants under Persian kings. Yet God has shown them kindness and let them rebuild. Ezra fears this small survival could be lost (verse 14). Deuteronomy 7:3–4 gives the law’s stated concern: turning to other gods.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects these marriages with worship of other gods. Ezra gives no personal testimony from the wives. How does Ezra describe his people’s condition in verse 9?

events.title: The marriage investigation
events.summary: While Ezra prays and weeps, a large crowd gathers and weeps with him. Shecaniah proposes a covenant to send away the foreign wives and their children. Ezra makes the leaders swear to it. All the men are called to Jerusalem within three days. They sit in the open square, trembling in heavy rain. Family heads are chosen to examine each case. The work takes three months. The book ends with a list of the men, and some had children.
events.detail: The proposal in verse 3 comes from Shecaniah, not from Ezra. It covers the wives and “those who are born of them.” Verse 15 records four men who opposed the plan. No word from God is reported approving it. The women and children do not speak anywhere in the chapter. The last verse mentions children and then stops (verse 44). Elsewhere the Bible honors Ruth, a woman of Moab (Ruth 4:13–17).

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Persian royal road
ancientRoads.summary: Persian kings kept a road with rest stations from Sardis to Susa. Herodotus counted 111 stations on it.
ancientRoads.detail: Royal messengers changed horses at the stations. Esther 8:10 sends the king’s letters by riders on royal horses.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Herodotus names lands and rivers, not towns. The line between Sardis and Susa is a broad guide.

regions.name: Persian Empire · part shown
regions.summary: Cyrus founded the Persian Empire in 550 BCE and took Babylon in 539 BCE. It reached from Egypt and Asia Minor to the Indus Valley.
regions.detail: Persian kings let Judeans go home and rebuild the temple (Ezra 1; 6). Nehemiah serves the king at Susa.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows only the western part of the empire. Its eastern lands lie off this map.

regions.name: Yehud · Persian province of Judah
regions.summary: Yehud was the Persian province around Jerusalem. It ran from the western foothills to the Dead Sea.
regions.detail: Zerubbabel and Jeshua rebuild the temple here. Nehemiah, as governor, rebuilds Jerusalem’s wall.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the land around Jerusalem.

regions.name: Samaria · Persian province
regions.summary: Samaria stayed a seat of government under Assyria, Babylon, and Persia.
regions.detail: Officials in Samaria write to the king against the builders (Ezra 4). Sanballat mocks the wall before the army of Samaria (Nehemiah 4:2).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province north of Yehud.

guides.title: Ezra: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Return occurs within Persian rule
steps.text: Verse 1 credits the LORD with moving a foreign king. Verse 3 makes the return a matter of choice: “Whoever there is among you.” Verse 5 says those went whose spirit God had stirred. Permission comes from the ruler of the whole region. No king of Judah is restored, and worship resumes without independence. Verses 7–11 count the old vessels to link the new house with the first. The Cyrus Cylinder provides wider royal context without naming Judah’s returning families.

steps.title: A stored record changes a local dispute
steps.text: The search begins in Babylon, and the record turns up in Media (verses 1–2). A clay bulla of the Persian period shows how documents were sealed. A stored memo answers the charges of local opponents. Darius goes beyond what the Jews asked and pays the costs (verses 8–9). In verse 10 he wants prayers for himself and his sons. So permission brings duties and royal oversight with it. Verse 14 credits the result to prophets, God’s command, and Persian kings together.

steps.title: A boundary decision has a human cost
steps.text: The proposal in verse 3 comes from Shecaniah, not from Ezra. It covers the wives and “those who are born of them.” Verse 15 records four men who opposed the plan. No word from God is reported approving it. The women and children do not speak anywhere in the chapter. The last verse mentions children and then stops (verse 44). Elsewhere the Bible honors Ruth, a woman of Moab (Ruth 4:13–17).

chapterMaps.narrative: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, the LORD stirs the king’s spirit. Cyrus sends a written order through his kingdom. He says the God of heaven has told him to build a house in Jerusalem. Any of God’s people may go up and build it. Their neighbors are to help with silver, gold, goods, and animals. Family heads, priests, and Levites prepare to go. Cyrus brings out the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar took. They are counted out to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah.

Priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants follow. Some families cannot prove that they belong to Israel. Some priests cannot find their family records. The governor bars them from the holy food until a priest can decide. The whole company numbers 42,360, with servants and singers besides. Family heads give gold, silver, and priestly garments for the work.

chapterMaps.narrative: The prophets Haggai and Zechariah speak to the Jews in God’s name. Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin again to build the house. Tattenai, the governor west of the River, asks who authorized them. He takes down the builders’ names. The work continues while he writes to King Darius. His letter reports the elders’ answer in full. They say Cyrus ordered the house rebuilt and returned its vessels. Tattenai asks the king to search the royal archives.

chapterMaps.narrative: Darius orders a search of the archives. A scroll is found in the fortress of Achmetha in Media. It records Cyrus’s decree, with the temple’s size and the crown’s payment. Darius tells Tattenai to leave the work alone. He orders the costs paid from the region’s taxes. He supplies animals, wheat, salt, wine, and oil for the offerings. The elders finish the house in the sixth year of Darius. They dedicate it with joy and keep the Passover.

chapterMaps.narrative: Years later Ezra comes up from Babylon. He is a priest of Aaron’s line and a scribe skilled in Moses’s law. King Artaxerxes grants all he asks. The journey takes about four months. The king’s letter lets any Israelite go with him. It sends silver and gold for offerings and frees temple workers from tax. It tells Ezra to appoint judges and teach God’s laws. Ezra blesses the LORD, who put this in the king’s heart.

chapterMaps.narrative: Ezra lists the family heads who travel with him. At the river Ahava he finds no Levites in the camp. He sends for some, and Levites and temple servants join. He calls a fast and asks God for a safe road. He is ashamed to ask the king for soldiers. He weighs the silver, gold, and vessels into the hands of twelve priests. They reach Jerusalem safely. On the fourth day everything is weighed again and written down.

chapterMaps.narrative: Leaders tell Ezra that the people have married among the neighboring peoples. Priests, Levites, and officials are among them. Ezra tears his clothes and sits appalled until the evening offering. Then he kneels and prays. He says the people’s guilt has grown up to the heavens. God has given them a little relief and a foothold in his holy place. They are still servants under Persia’s kings. He asks how they can break the commandments again.

chapterMaps.narrative: While Ezra prays and weeps, a large crowd gathers and weeps with him. Shecaniah proposes a covenant to send away the foreign wives and their children. Ezra makes the leaders swear to it. All the men are called to Jerusalem within three days. They sit in the open square, trembling in heavy rain. Family heads are chosen to examine each case. The work takes three months. The book ends with a list of the men, and some had children.
